claims.text: The as-printed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a monolithic fcc matrix.
Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti are homogeneously distributed in the as-printed alloy.
The starting alloy has demonstrated high strength.
The starting alloy has demonstrated fatigue resistance.
High-temperature degradation is governed by selective elemental diffusion from the fcc matrix.
Selective elemental diffusion drives formation of a dual-layer surface scale.
Under oxidizing conditions, preferential outward diffusion of Cr produces a Cr-rich oxide scale.
The Cr-rich oxide formed under oxidizing conditions is continuous, adherent, and protective.
A protective Cr-rich oxide slows degradation and stabilizes the underlying material.
Under reducing conditions, lower oxygen activity and modified diffusion kinetics prevent stable Cr-oxide formation.
Reducing conditions favor formation of a Ti-rich or mixed oxide scale.
The Ti-rich or mixed oxide scale formed under reducing conditions is less adherent and less protective than the Cr-rich scale.
The less-protective scale under reducing conditions spalls more readily.
Greater oxide spallation under reducing conditions causes accelerated surface degradation relative to oxidizing conditions.
The bulk fcc matrix remains largely intact during both types of exposure.
The proposed comparison uses matched exposures at 800°C–900°C in oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres while holding pressure, geometry, duration, and thermal-mechanical conditions constant.
The hypothesis is restricted to 800°C–900°C exposures that do not induce bulk transformation of the fcc matrix.
Similar scale composition, adherence, and degradation rates in the two atmospheres would falsify the proposed selective-diffusion mechanism.
